newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila defers arraignment of Chinese fishermen.
newsitem.headline: Manila defers arraignment of Chinese fishermen.

text.p: A Philippine judge on Friday postponed a hearing on illegal entry charges against 21 Chinese fishermen caught in a disputed part of the South China Sea after they questioned Manila's authority over the area.

The lawyer for the Chinese fishermen said Manila could not try them because the Scarborough Shoal, a rock formation which Manila says is within its 200-mile exclusive economic zone, is not part of Philippine territory.
Beijing says the shoal and all other islets, reefs and rocks in the South China Sea historically belong to China.
Government prosecutor Jesus Llamado said he would check on the claims of the fishermen that they were not allowed enough time to formally reply to the charges.

Early this month, Philippine foreign affairs undersecretary Rodolfo Severino said the national committee on illegal entrants would ask government prosecutors to withdraw the charges against the Chinese and instead file a case of illegal fishing.
Under the United Nations Convention on Law of the Sea, foreign vessels can pass through a country's exclusive economic zone provided they do not exploit resources in the area, he said.
Judge Eliodoro Ubiadas ordered the Chinese to file within five days their petition to dismiss the illegal entry charges against them.
The Chinese are also facing separate charges of illegal fishing.
Nineteen of the 21 Chinese, who were arrested by Philippine police in the shoal on May 20, appeared in court on Friday.
Their arrest sparked the third diplomatic row during May between Manila and Beijing over the barely visible outcrop.

China earlier protested against the hoisting by Filipinos of their national flag over the rocks. It protested again when a group of Philippine congressmen sailed to the shoal to be photographed standing under the flag.
